questions.q: Which one of the following subjects was transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
questions.e: The 42nd Amendment moved five subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice. Public health, prisons and local government remain State List subjects.
questions.h: Five moved: E-F-W-W-A (Education, Forests, Weights, Wild animals, Administration of justice).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Parliament's power to legislate on a State List subject under Article 249:
1. The Rajya Sabha must pass a resolution supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting.
2. The resolution remains in force for a period not exceeding one year, and may be renewed from time to time.
3. A law made under it ceases to have effect six months after the resolution ceases to be in force.
4. The resolution must also be passed by the Lok Sabha.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 249 is a special power of the Rajya Sabha as the House of the States, which declares that national interest requires central legislation. The Lok Sabha is not required to adopt the resolution, so statement 4 is wrong.
questions.h: Rajya Sabha speaks for States; its 2/3 vote lets the Centre enter their list.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 252 of the Constitution:
1. Parliament may legislate on a State List subject if the Legislatures of two or more States pass resolutions requesting it to do so.
2. A law so made applies to the requesting States and to any other State that later adopts it by a resolution.
3. Such a law can be amended or repealed by the Legislature of any State to which it applies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Under Article 252 only Parliament can amend or repeal the law, which is why the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 could not be altered by individual States. Statement 3 therefore fails.

questions.q:
Statement-I: A State law on a Concurrent List subject that is repugnant to an earlier Union law can prevail in that State.
Statement-II: Article 254(2) allows this if the State Bill has been reserved for the President and has received his assent.
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Both are correct and the second explains the first. Even so, Parliament may later override the State law by legislating on the same matter, since the proviso to Article 254(2) preserves its power to add to, amend, vary or repeal.

questions.q: The doctrine under which a law is examined for its true nature and character, to decide under which List it falls even if it incidentally trenches on a subject in another List, is known as the doctrine of
questions.e: Pith and substance looks at the real subject of the enactment, and incidental encroachment does not invalidate it. Colourable legislation is the opposite: doing indirectly what cannot be done directly.

questions.q:
Parliament can make laws on a subject in the State List in which of the following situations?
1. When a Proclamation of National Emergency is in operation.
2. When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a simple majority declaring it to be in the national interest.
3. When President's Rule is imposed in a State, in respect of that State.
4. When the Governor of a State requests Parliament to do so.
How many of the situations given above are correct?
questions.e: The Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 needs a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, and there is no provision for a Governor's request. National Emergency (Article 250) and President's Rule (Article 356) are valid occasions.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Seventh Schedule:
1. Marriage and divorce are in the Concurrent List.
2. Census is in the Union List.
3. Public health and sanitation are in the State List.
4. Police is in the Concurrent List.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Police, along with public order, is a State List subject, so statement 4 is wrong. Marriage and divorce (Concurrent), census (Union) and public health (State) are correctly placed.

questions.q: Which of the following Acts was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 on the basis of resolutions passed by State Legislatures?
o: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
questions.e: The Water Act, 1974 was passed under Article 252 after State resolutions. The Air Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 were enacted to implement the 1972 Stockholm decisions under Article 253, and the Forest Act is a colonial law.

questions.q: Which Article empowers Parliament to make laws on any subject, including those in the State List, for implementing treaties, agreements or conventions with other countries?
questions.e: Article 253 gives Parliament this power with no consent of the States, since foreign affairs and treaty obligations belong to the Union. Articles 249, 250 and 252 are the other routes into the State List and each has a different trigger.

questions.q:
Arrange the following Constitutional Amendments in chronological order:
1. 80th Amendment, shifting to the scheme of sharing all Union taxes with States
2. 42nd Amendment, transferring subjects to the Concurrent List
3. 101st Amendment, introducing GST
4. 7th Amendment, reorganisation of States
questions.e: The order is the 7th (1956), 42nd (1976), 80th (2000) and 101st (2016) Amendments. Each reshaped Union-State relations in a different way: territory, subjects, revenue sharing and indirect taxation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 3 of the Constitution:
1. Parliament may by law form a new State or alter the area, boundaries or name of an existing State.
2. A Bill for this purpose can be introduced only on the recommendation of the President.
3. The views of the concerned State Legislature, when referred by the President, are binding on Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The President refers the Bill to the State Legislature only to ascertain its views, and Parliament is free to accept or reject them. This simple-majority power over States' territory is a unitary feature of Indian federalism.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the administrative relations between the Union and the States:
1. Article 256 requires the executive power of every State to be exercised so as to ensure compliance with laws made by Parliament.
2. Article 257 empowers the Union to give directions to a State regarding the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared to be of national or military importance.
3. If a State fails to comply with the Union's directions, the President may hold that a situation has arisen in which the State Government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: All three are correct; the third is Article 365, which can lead to a Proclamation under Article 356. The scheme ensures that the Centre can enforce its laws and directions through the States' own administrations.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under Article 258(1), the President may entrust Union functions to a State without the consent of that State.
2. Under Article 258A, the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Union Government, entrust State functions to the Union.
3. Parliament may, by law, confer powers and impose duties on a State or its officers in respect of a Union law even where the matter is not enumerated in the Union List.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 258(1) needs the State Government's consent, so statement 1 is wrong. Article 258(2) gives Parliament its own route, and 258A, added in 1956, allows State-to-Union entrustment.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131:
1. It covers disputes between the Government of India and one or more States.
2. It covers disputes between two or more States.
3. It does not cover disputes arising from a pre-Constitution treaty or agreement that continues in operation.
4. It covers disputes between a private citizen and a State Government.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 131 is for federal disputes involving a question on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends. A private citizen cannot invoke it, and the pre-Constitution treaty exclusion is also correct.

questions.q: The duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance, and to ensure that the government of every State is carried on in accordance with the Constitution, is laid down in Article
questions.e: Article 355 is the source of the duty, while Article 356 is the remedy when a State's constitutional machinery fails. Article 365 deals with a State's failure to comply with Union directions.

questions.q: Which Article provides that full faith and credit shall be given throughout the territory of India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State?
questions.e: Article 261 is the Inter-State comity provision, and it lets a judgment given in one State be enforced elsewhere. Article 262 concerns river water disputes and Article 263 the Inter-State Council.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Inter-State Council:
1. Article 263 empowers the President to establish it if it appears that the public interest would be served.
2. It was established in 1990 on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission.
3. It adjudicates legal disputes between States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Council can inquire into and advise on disputes, discuss common interests and recommend coordination, but it cannot adjudicate; legal disputes between States go to the Supreme Court under Article 131.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Zonal Councils:
1. They were created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and are statutory, not constitutional, bodies.
2. The Chief Minister of the host State presides as the permanent Chairman of each Zonal Council.
3. They are advisory bodies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Union Home Minister is the common Chairman of the five Zonal Councils, and Chief Ministers serve as Vice-Chairmen by rotation. The Councils are advisory bodies created in 1956 to ease post-reorganisation tensions.

questions.q:
Consider the following pairs:
Category of revenue : Article
1. Duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States : Article 268
2. Taxes levied and collected by the Union and distributed between the Union and the States : Article 270
3. GST on inter-State supplies levied and collected by the Union and apportioned : Article 269A
4. Statutory grants-in-aid to needy States : Article 282
How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.e: Statutory grants-in-aid are under Article 275, while Article 282 provides discretionary grants for public purposes. The other three pairs are correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about devolution recommended by recent Finance Commissions:
1. The 14th Finance Commission raised the States' share of the divisible pool of Union taxes from 32 per cent to 42 per cent.
2. The 15th Finance Commission recommended 41 per cent for the period 2021-22 to 2025-26, adjusting for the creation of the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
3. The 15th Finance Commission kept the States' share at 42 per cent.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The 14th Commission's jump to 42 per cent was a major boost to States' untied resources. The 15th Commission trimmed it to 41 per cent, setting aside one per cent for the new Union Territories.
questions.s: Reports of the 14th and 15th Finance Commissions; Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy
questions.h: 14th: 42; 15th: 41 (1 per cent for J&K and Ladakh).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Finance Commission under Article 280:
1. It is constituted by the President at the expiration of every fifth year or earlier.
2. It consists of a Chairman and four other members.
3. Its recommendations are binding on the Government of India.
4. The Chairman must be a retired Judge of the Supreme Court.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statements 1 and 2 follow Article 280. The recommendations are advisory and are laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum, and Parliament, not the Constitution, decides the qualifications of members.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Goods and Services Tax Council:
1. The Union Finance Minister is its Chairperson.
2. The quorum for its meetings is one-half of the total number of its members.
3. Decisions are taken by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting.
4. The vote of the Central Government has a weightage of one-third of the total votes cast, and the votes of all States taken together two-thirds.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: All four follow Article 279A. The three-fourths rule means the Centre can block any decision with its one-third weight, and the States can block it only by acting together.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapter on GST Council; Constitution, Article 279A
questions.h: 1/3 Centre, 2/3 States, 3/4 to pass: Centre can veto alone.

questions.q:
Statement-I: The 101st Constitutional Amendment gave both Parliament and State Legislatures the power to make laws on GST.
Statement-II: Parliament has exclusive power to make laws on GST on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Article 246A provides concurrent power over GST, with an exclusive Parliamentary power for inter-State supplies. The second statement qualifies rather than explains the first, so it is a correct but non-explanatory statement.
questions.s: Constitution, Article 246A; Laxmikanth, chapter on GST

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the immunity of property from taxation:
1. The property of the Union is exempt from taxes imposed by a State or any authority within a State, subject to Article 285.
2. The property and income of a State are exempt from Union taxation.
3. Parliament cannot, even by law, tax a trade or business carried on by a State Government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Articles 285 and 289 give reciprocal immunity. Article 289(2) lets Parliament tax a State's commercial activities by law, so statement 3 is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about borrowing under the Constitution:
1. The Union may borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India within limits fixed by Parliament.
2. A State may borrow from foreign countries on the security of its Consolidated Fund without any permission.
3. A State requires the Union's consent to raise any loan if a loan made or guaranteed by the Union is still outstanding.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 293(1) lets a State borrow only within the territory of India, and foreign borrowing is a Union matter. Article 293(3) is the debt-control lever that gives the Centre a say in State borrowing.

questions.q: Which Article empowers the Union or a State to make grants for any public purpose, even if that purpose is not one on which Parliament or the State Legislature may make laws?
questions.e: Article 282 is the basis of discretionary grants, such as the Plan grants once given through the Planning Commission. Article 275 provides statutory grants on the Finance Commission's advice.

questions.q:
Match the following Finance Commissions with their Chairmen:
List-I
A. Twelfth Finance Commission
B. Thirteenth Finance Commission
C. Fourteenth Finance Commission
D. Fifteenth Finance Commission
List-II
1. N.K. Singh
2. Y.V. Reddy
3. Vijay Kelkar
4. C. Rangarajan
questions.e: The chairmen were C. Rangarajan (12th), Vijay Kelkar (13th), Y.V. Reddy (14th) and N.K. Singh (15th). Each Commission serves a five-year award period.
questions.s: Reports of the Finance Commissions; Ramesh Singh, Indian Economy

questions.q: In the 15th Finance Commission's formula for horizontal distribution of the divisible pool among States, which criterion carried the highest weight?
questions.e: Income distance carried 45 per cent, population 15 per cent, area 15 per cent, forest and ecology 10 per cent, demographic performance 12.5 per cent and tax effort 2.5 per cent. The heavy income-distance weight favours poorer States.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the divisible pool of Union taxes:
1. The net proceeds of any cess levied by the Union for specific purposes do not form part of the divisible pool.
2. The proceeds of surcharge on income tax are shared with the States.
3. Corporation tax is part of the divisible pool.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Under Articles 270 and 271 cess and surcharge proceeds stay with the Union, which is why a rising share of cess and surcharge shrinks the States' effective share. Corporation tax is an important component of the pool.

questions.q: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act provided for compensation to States for loss of revenue arising from GST for a period of up to
questions.e: The compensation window was five years from the introduction of GST on 1 July 2017, to ease the transition for States giving up their independent power to tax goods and services.
questions.s: Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016; Laxmikanth, chapter on GST

questions.q: Under the Constitution as amended by the 101st Amendment, which of the following remains outside the levy of GST and may continue to be taxed by States?
questions.e: Alcohol for human consumption is wholly excluded, so States can tax it as before. Tobacco is under GST, and petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas and ATF come under GST only from a date the Council recommends.
questions.s: Laxmikanth, chapter on GST; Constitution, Article 366(12A)

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse:
1. Article 301 guarantees such freedom only within a State.
2. Parliament may impose restrictions on freedom of trade between States in the public interest.
3. A State Bill imposing reasonable restrictions on trade in the public interest requires the previous sanction of the President for its introduction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 301 guarantees freedom throughout the territory of India, not just within a State. Articles 302 and 304(b) allow Parliament's restrictions and State restrictions with the President's previous sanction, preventing economic fragmentation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Sarkaria Commission:
1. It was set up in 1983 under Justice R.S. Sarkaria to review Centre-State relations.
2. It recommended the setting up of a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263.
3. It recommended the deletion of Article 356 from the Constitution.
4. It recommended that the Governor be appointed after consultation with the Chief Minister of the State concerned.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The Commission proposed that Article 356 be used very sparingly as a last resort, not that it be deleted. It also suggested that the Governor be an eminent outsider appointed after consulting the Chief Minister.

questions.q: Which commission, set up in 2007 under a former Chief Justice of India, re-examined Centre-State relations?
o: National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution
questions.e: The Madan Mohan Punchhi Commission reported in 2010. The Venkatachaliah Commission (NCRWC) was also headed by a former Chief Justice but was set up in 2000 for a general constitutional review.

questions.q:
Match the following bodies with their details:
List-I
A. Sarkaria Commission
B. Rajamannar Committee
C. Punchhi Commission
D. First Administrative Reforms Commission
List-II
1. Appointed by the Tamil Nadu Government in 1969
2. Set up in 1983 under a retired Supreme Court judge
3. Set up in 2007 under a former Chief Justice of India
4. Set up in 1966, initially headed by Morarji Desai
questions.e: Each reviewed Union-State relations in a different era. Morarji Desai headed the first ARC until he became Deputy Prime Minister, and K. Hanumanthaiya then took over.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about river water disputes:
1. Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication of disputes relating to inter-State rivers or river valleys.
2. Parliament may by law exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts over such disputes.
3. The River Boards Act, 1956 led to the constitution of River Boards for several inter-State rivers.
4. Under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act as amended in 2002, a tribunal must submit its report within three years, extendable by two years.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The River Boards Act, 1956 was enacted but no River Board was ever set up, so statement 3 is wrong. Article 262 and the 2002 amendment's time limits are correct, and the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 uses the ouster power under Article 262(2).

questions.q:
Statement-I: NITI Aayog is neither a constitutional nor a statutory body.
Statement-II: NITI Aayog was set up by a resolution of the Union Cabinet on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission.
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Both are correct and the second explains the first, since a Cabinet resolution creates an executive body with no constitutional or parliamentary backing. The Planning Commission was set up the same way in 1950.
questions.s: NITI Aayog; Laxmikanth, chapter on Non-Constitutional Bodies

questions.q:
Arrange the following Centre-State review bodies in chronological order of their appointment:
1. Punchhi Commission
2. Rajamannar Committee
3. National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution
4. Sarkaria Commission
questions.e: The order is Rajamannar (1969), Sarkaria (1983), the NCRWC (2000) and Punchhi (2007).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a National Emergency under Article 352 after the 44th Amendment:
1. It can be proclaimed on the grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
2. The President can proclaim it only on the written recommendation of the Union Cabinet.
3. 'Internal disturbance' remains a ground for proclamation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: After the 1975 misuse, the 44th Amendment replaced the vague 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' and required the Cabinet's written recommendation. These safeguards stop one person from invoking the extraordinary powers.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a Proclamation of National Emergency:
1. It must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month.
2. The approval requires a special majority, namely a majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of the members present and voting.
3. Once approved, it continues for six months and can be extended indefinitely by repeated six-monthly approvals.
4. It can be revoked only after Parliament passes a resolution to that effect.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The President can revoke a Proclamation at any time by a subsequent Proclamation, without Parliament's approval. The other three statements are correct, and there is no ceiling on the duration of an Emergency.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Lok Sabha's control over a National Emergency:
1. A resolution to disapprove or discontinue the Emergency can be passed by a simple majority of the Lok Sabha.
2. If one-tenth of the Lok Sabha's members give written notice, a special sitting must be held within fourteen days to consider such a resolution.
3. The Rajya Sabha can also revoke the Proclamation by passing a similar resolution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: These safeguards were added by the 44th Amendment; only the Lok Sabha has the power to force revocation, reflecting its position as the directly elected House.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the effect of a National Emergency on Fundamental Rights:
1. Under Article 358, the freedoms under Article 19 are automatically suspended when the Emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression.
2. Under Article 358, Article 19 is automatically suspended also when the Emergency is declared on the ground of armed rebellion.
3. Under Article 359, the President cannot suspend the enforcement of the rights guaranteed by Articles 20 and 21.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The 44th Amendment limited automatic suspension of Article 19 to Emergencies on grounds of war or external aggression, and made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable under Article 359.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about President's Rule under Article 356:
1. A Proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month.
2. It can ordinarily be continued for a maximum period of three years through six-monthly approvals.
3. Continuation beyond one year requires that a National Emergency be in operation and that the Election Commission certify that continuation is necessary.
4. It is approved by a special majority of both Houses.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Approval must come within two months, not one, and by a simple majority, not a special one. Statements 2 and 3 are the 44th Amendment's rules on duration.

questions.q:
Which of the following was laid down by the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) regarding Article 356?
1. A Proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
2. The President may dissolve the State Assembly immediately on proclaiming President's Rule, without waiting for Parliament's approval.
3. Secularism is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Select the correct answer.
questions.e: Bommai held that the Assembly can only be suspended until Parliament approves the Proclamation; dissolution before approval is not permitted. The ruling made the misuse of Article 356 harder and treated a State government's secular conduct as a constitutional requirement.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a Financial Emergency under Article 360:
1. It can be proclaimed if the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened.
2. It must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month.
3. Like a National Emergency, it must be renewed every six months.
4. During it, the President cannot reduce the salaries of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Approval is required within two months, and once approved a Financial Emergency continues until revoked, with no six-monthly renewal. The President may direct salary reductions for all classes of persons serving the Union, including judges. It has never been proclaimed.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the National Emergencies in India:
1. The first Proclamation was made in October 1962 on the ground of external aggression.
2. The Proclamation of 1962 was revoked in 1963 after the ceasefire.
3. The Proclamation of June 1975 was made on the ground of internal disturbance.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: The 1962 Proclamation, made during the China war, was revoked only in January 1968. The 1975 Proclamation on the ground of 'internal disturbance' coexisted with the 1971 one and both were revoked in March 1977.

questions.q:
Statement-I: During a National Emergency, the federal structure of the Constitution is transformed into a virtually unitary one.
Statement-II: The Union executive may give directions to any State on how to exercise its executive power, and Parliament may legislate on State List subjects.
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Articles 353 and 250 concentrate executive and legislative authority in the Union, which is why the system turns unitary. The Union may even modify the sharing of revenues under Article 354.

questions.q: A Proclamation under Article 356 is issued when the Lok Sabha stands dissolved, and the Rajya Sabha approves it within two months. The Proclamation will
o: Lapse immediately because the Lok Sabha cannot approve it
Continue for six months regardless of the Lok Sabha
Continue for one year without approval by the Lok Sabha
Continue until thirty days after the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha, unless it approves the Proclamation before that
questions.e: The proviso to Article 356(3) protects the Proclamation during a dissolution if the Rajya Sabha has approved it. The new Lok Sabha must then approve it within thirty days of its first sitting, or it lapses.

questions.q:
Statement-I: In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), a majority of the Supreme Court held that detainees could not seek habeas corpus during the Emergency to challenge preventive detention.
Statement-II: The 44th Amendment provides that the rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359.
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Both are correct. The 44th Amendment, passed after the Emergency, responded to the climate that the ruling represented, although Statement-II does not explain the 1976 ruling. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented in the case.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the exercise of legislative powers during President's Rule:
1. The President may declare that the powers of the State Legislature shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.
2. A law made by Parliament in such a situation continues in force after the Proclamation ceases, until altered or repealed by the competent Legislature.
3. The President may assume the powers of the State High Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Article 356(1)(c) bars the President from assuming the powers of a High Court, preserving judicial independence. Article 357(2) keeps laws made by Parliament or the President alive after the Proclamation ceases.
